Nature reserve “Westrup Heath” at the flowering of the heath, Haltern am See, North Rhine-Westphalia, Germany
The Westrup Heath (sometimes referred to locally as the “Flaesheim Heath”) is a nature reserve in Haltern am See between the Haltern reservoir and the Westrup hamlet, from which it takes its name. The area is bordered by Federal Highway 58 to the north and State Highway 652 to the east. Along the roads, there are narrow strips of forest that serve as protective buffers. To the southwest is a sand extraction area. The remaining area of the sand heaths that once dominated the Haltern region lies on a post-glacial dune landscape. In order to preserve the once extensive heathland for future generations and to ensure that it can continue to be enjoyed, part of it was placed under nature conservation in 1936.

Dortmund-Ems Canal (from the bridge of the county road 23) in the hamlet Berenbrock, Lüdinghausen, North Rhine-Westphalia, Germany
The idea of connecting the industrial conurbation of the Ruhr region with a navigable waterway to the North Sea, namely the seaport of Emden, arose in the 19th century because the rapidly growing volume of freight traffic was overloading the railways and cheaper transport was needed.
Construction of the Dortmund-Ems Canal began in 1892 and took around seven years. On August 11, 1899, the canal was officially opened by Emperor Wilhelm II – as the first large, uniformly planned inland waterway canal in Germany.
Due to its strategic importance during World War II, the canal was attacked and damaged several times, which temporarily interrupted its use. After the war, it was repaired and gradually modernized to accommodate larger ships and push barges.
The Dortmund-Ems Canal is approximately 269 kilometers long and runs from Dortmund to the Ems estuary port near Emden. It connects to other important canals at various points, including the Wesel-Datteln Canal, the Datteln-Hamm Canal, and the Mittelland Canal network, making it a central hub of the German waterway system.
One of the most famous engineering structures is the old ship lift at Henrichenburg near Waltrop. It overcame a height difference of 14 meters and enabled ship traffic between different sections of the canal.
